problemText: Which of these samples is a pure ELEMENT?
choices: Stainless steel, a uniform blend of iron, chromium, and nickel
Neon gas sealed inside a lighted sign
Ammonia, NH₃
Muddy river water with silt suspended in it
hints: An element contains only ONE kind of atom and cannot be broken down by any chemical reaction.

problemText: Gray iron filings are stirred into yellow powdered sulfur. The gray specks are still clearly visible among the yellow powder, and dragging a magnet through the pile pulls the iron back out. How should this sample be classified?
choices: Compound, because iron and sulfur are now combined into one material
Element, because iron and sulfur are both elements
Heterogeneous mixture — the two solids are unbonded and you can point to visibly different regions
Homogeneous mixture, because stirring spread the two powders evenly
hints: A magnet is a PHYSICAL tool — anything it can undo was never chemically bonded.
Once you know it is a mixture, ask whether you can see regions of different composition.

problemText: Which of these samples is a HOMOGENEOUS MIXTURE?
choices: Vinegar — acetic acid fully dissolved in water, uniform throughout, and the strength can be adjusted
Dry ice, solid CO₂
A length of copper wire
Olive oil floating in a layer on top of water
hints: First decide pure or mixed: can the recipe be adjusted, or is the composition locked?
Then ask whether you could point at visibly different regions inside the sample.

problemText: Two sealed flasks sit on a bench. Flask 1 is labeled H₂O. Flask 2 is labeled H₂ + O₂. Both contents are colorless and look perfectly uniform. What is the correct classification of each?
choices: Both are compounds, because both flasks contain hydrogen and oxygen
Flask 1 is a mixture and Flask 2 is a compound
Flask 1 is a compound and Flask 2 is a homogeneous mixture of two elements
Both are homogeneous mixtures, because both look uniform
hints: One chemical formula with no plus sign means the atoms are chemically bonded.
A plus sign between two formulas means two separate substances happen to share the same container — nothing is bonded, so the ratio is adjustable.

problemText: A colorless liquid is gently boiled. The vapor is collected and condenses into pure water, and a dry white solid is left behind in the flask. Which conclusion about the original liquid is best supported?
choices: It was a compound, because it came apart into two different substances
It was an element, because elements are the only substances that boil cleanly
It was a heterogeneous mixture, because two substances were recovered from it
It was a homogeneous mixture, because a purely physical change — boiling — separated it into two substances
hints: Ask what kind of change boiling is, and what kind of change is required to break a compound apart.

Compounds only come apart in a chemical reaction; anything separable by boiling, filtering, or a magnet was a mixture. The liquid looked uniform before boiling, which fixes the second half of the label.

problemText: Every sample of a certain compound of hydrogen and oxygen contains exactly 8.0 g of oxygen for each 1.0 g of hydrogen, no matter where on Earth the sample came from. A chemist fully decomposes a 27.0 g sample of this compound. How many grams of oxygen are released? Type your answer as a number.
hints: A compound has a FIXED mass ratio, so the 8.0 : 1.0 split holds for a sample of any size.
8.0 g of oxygen plus 1.0 g of hydrogen makes 9.0 g of compound; 27.0 g is three of those portions.

problemText: Which of these is a CHEMICAL property of iron?
choices: Its silvery gray color
Its density of 7.87 g/cm³
Its ability to rust when left in damp air
Its melting point of 1538 °C
hints: A chemical property can only be observed by letting the substance stop being itself.

problemText: Which of these everyday events is a PHYSICAL change?
choices: Candle wax melting and pooling around the wick
A silver spoon slowly turning black with tarnish
Baking soda fizzing when vinegar is poured on it
A firework burning with a bright green flame
hints: Run the identity test on each: after the event, is the starting substance still chemically the same substance?
Three of the four produce substances that did not exist beforehand. One only changes state.

problemText: Which pair lists TWO properties that are both intensive — that is, both independent of how much of the sample you have?
choices: Mass and volume
Volume and melting point
Length and mass
Boiling point and density
hints: Imagine cutting the sample in half. Which listed values would change, and which would stay the same?
Mass, volume, and length all shrink when you cut the sample; the other two do not.

problemText: A student watches bubbles form in two containers: (1) a pot of water held at a steady 100 °C on a stove, and (2) a chunk of limestone, CaCO₃, dropped into cold hydrochloric acid, which releases CO₂ gas. Which statement classifies the two events correctly?
choices: Both are chemical changes, because gas is produced in both
Container 1 is a physical change and container 2 is a chemical change — the gas leaving the pot is still H₂O, while the CO₂ gas did not exist as CO₂ a moment earlier
Both are physical changes, because bubbling is only a change of state
Container 1 is a chemical change and container 2 is a physical change, because heating always drives a reaction
hints: Bubbles alone prove nothing. The useful question is whether the escaping gas is a NEW substance.
Steam is the same H₂O that was in the pot; the carbon dioxide had to be built out of the limestone and the acid.

problemText: A 12.0 g piece of wood is burned in an open dish, and only 0.9 g of ash is left behind. A student concludes that mass was destroyed. Which explanation is correct?
choices: Mass really is destroyed during burning, which is why ash always weighs less than the fuel
Wood is a mixture, and conservation of mass applies only to pure substances
Conservation of mass applies only to physical changes, never to chemical reactions
Mass was conserved — carbon dioxide and water vapor formed and drifted away into the room, and nobody weighed them
hints: Atoms are never created or destroyed. If the products weigh less, ask where some of them went.
The dish is open to the air, so any gaseous product escapes before the balance sees it.

problemText: Inside a sealed steel flask, 8.0 g of methane, CH₄, burns completely in 32.0 g of oxygen gas. The only products are 22.0 g of carbon dioxide and some water. What mass of water, in grams, is produced? Type your answer as a number.
hints: The flask is sealed, so nothing enters or leaves: total mass of reactants = total mass of products.
Add both reactant masses to get the total, then subtract the 22.0 g of carbon dioxide.

problemText: How many significant figures are in the measurement 0.00830 g?
hints: Leading zeros only hold the decimal point in place; start counting at the first nonzero digit, and remember a trailing zero counts when a decimal point is written.

problemText: A rectangular piece of foil is measured as 6.0 cm by 4.25 cm. What is its area, correctly reported?
choices: 25.5 cm²
26 cm²
25 cm²
hints: Area is a multiplication, so the fewest-SIGNIFICANT-FIGURES rule applies.
6.0 has 2 sig figs and 4.25 has 3. The raw product is 25.5 — round it to 2 significant figures.

problemText: A chemist masses three portions of a solid and adds them: 24.68 g + 3.1 g + 0.257 g. What is the total, correctly reported?
hints: This is addition, so the limiting question is DECIMAL PLACES, not significant-figure count.
3.1 g is known only to the tenths place, so the sum can be too. The raw total is 28.037 g.

problemText: A sample is recorded on a lab sheet as having a mass of 0.00450 kg. Which statement about this measurement is correct?
choices: Rewritten in grams it is 4.50 g, and the measurement has 3 significant figures
Rewritten in grams it is 4.5 g, and the measurement has 2 significant figures
It has 5 significant figures, because five digits are written after the decimal point
Rewritten in grams it is 450 g, and the measurement has 3 significant figures
hints: Changing the prefix rescales the number but never changes how certain the measurement was.
Count sig figs first: the two leading zeros are placeholders, the 4 and 5 count, and the trailing zero counts because a decimal point is written. Then convert with 1 kg = 1000 g.

problemText: An empty beaker has a mass of 68.4 g. Filled with a liquid, the beaker and liquid together have a mass of 145.27 g. Report the mass of the liquid alone, in grams, to the correct number of significant figures. Type your answer as a number.
hints: Subtraction follows the fewest-DECIMAL-PLACES rule, not the significant-figure rule.
145.27 − 68.4 = 76.87 on the calculator, but 68.4 is known only to the tenths place.

problemText: A student finds the density of a liquid. The empty graduated cylinder has a mass of 24.87 g. With the liquid in it, the cylinder has a mass of 45.2 g. The liquid occupies 25.0 mL. Which is the correctly reported density?
choices: 0.8 g/mL
hints: Two operations, two different rules: the subtraction that gives the liquid's mass is limited by decimal places, and the division that follows is limited by significant figures.
45.2 − 24.87 = 20.33, which must be reported to the tenths place as 20.3 g — that is 3 significant figures. Now divide by 25.0 mL, which also has 3.

problemText: A solid block with a density of 0.78 g/cm³ is dropped into a tank of water, whose density is 1.00 g/mL. What will the block do, and why?
choices: Float, because its density is less than the density of water
Sink, because every solid is denser than every liquid
Sink, because 0.78 g/cm³ is a smaller number and smaller numbers mean heavier packing
Stay suspended halfway down, because the two densities are fairly close
hints: Sinking or floating compares the object's mass PER UNIT VOLUME to the fluid's, not its total mass.

problemText: A sample of olive oil has a mass of 36.8 g and occupies a volume of 40.0 mL. What is its density?
hints: Density = mass ÷ volume. Check that the units you end up with are grams per milliliter.
Dividing volume by mass instead gives 1.09, which is the flipped answer — make sure grams sits on top.

problemText: A metal cube has a mass of 40.5 g. Dropped into a graduated cylinder holding 22.0 mL of water, it raises the water level to 37.0 mL. Reference densities in g/cm³: magnesium 1.74, aluminum 2.70, zinc 7.14, silver 10.5. Which metal is it? (1 mL = 1 cm³)
choices: Magnesium, 1.74 g/cm³
Aluminum, 2.70 g/cm³
Zinc, 7.14 g/cm³
Silver, 10.5 g/cm³
hints: Get the cube's volume by displacement: final water level minus initial water level.
The volume is 15.0 cm³. Divide 40.5 g by that and match the result to the reference list.

problemText: A crystal has a volume of 4.0 cm³. Convert this volume to cubic millimeters, given that 1 cm = 10 mm.
choices: 40 mm³
400 mm³
4000 mm³
0.40 mm³
hints: The conversion factor has to be applied to all three dimensions, so it gets cubed along with the unit.
1 cm³ = (10 mm)³ = 1000 mm³. Now scale that up to 4.0 cm³.

problemText: Mercury has a density of 13.6 g/mL. A procedure calls for 68.0 g of mercury, but the only glassware available measures volume. What volume should be measured out, and why?
choices: 924.8 mL, found by multiplying 68.0 g × 13.6 g/mL
5.00 mL, found by using the factor 1 mL / 13.6 g so that grams cancel
13.6 mL, because the density is the volume of any sample of mercury
68.0 mL, because 1 g of any liquid occupies 1 mL
hints: Write the units only and check what cancels: you start with grams and must finish with milliliters.
Multiplying grams by g/mL leaves g²/mL, a unit that does not exist — so the density factor has to be flipped.

problemText: A rectangular bar of an unknown metal measures 5.0 cm by 2.0 cm by 2.0 cm and has a mass of 0.1792 kg. What is its density in g/cm³? Type your answer as a number. (1 kg = 1000 g)
hints: The mass is in kilograms but the answer must be in grams per cubic centimeter — convert the mass first, using 1000 g / 1 kg.
The bar's volume is 5.0 × 2.0 × 2.0 = 20.0 cm³, and 0.1792 kg is 179.2 g. Now divide.
